Go-Future Trike Concept Is How One British Designer Envisions Us Shopping – Built With Plastic
10 photos
Photo: Yi-Chen Jung
Some vehicles are designed to reach breakneck speeds while others are designed for more practical purposes. Today, we explore a concept that belongs to the latter category, created for nothing more than helping urban dwellers carry their groceries home. It’s called the Tesco Go-Future and while it may not be some exotic vehicle or the wildest design, it is a concept that, frankly, may just have some method to its madness.
Folks, the Go-Future is nothing more than just a concept, one from the mind of Yi-Chen Jung, a designer from Coventry, UK. While it doesn’t actually exist, at least, not in the real world , what Mr. Jung has done here may actually stand a chance of being spotted in use some day, even if that ‘day’ is in the distant future.
Photo: Yi-Chen Jung Now, the purpose of the Go-Future is exactly what I mentioned, aimed at helping shoppers make it back home with their own private three-wheeling EV. Keep in mind that the Go-Future is presented as a ‘branded’ vehicle, and in this case, owned by Tesco but it’s not; the grocery store chain offers just a setting where we can see the Go-Future at work. That’s also where this story begins.
The grocery store, whichever actually ends up choosing such a vehicle to craft a fleet that places the shopper in the center of the action, acts as a hub for the Go-Future, which also means that it’s the place where they’ll be recharged after use and stored until the next user needs one.
One detail I couldn’t work out from the ideation page that Mr. Jung displays is how these babies make it back to home base; a story for another time. It is a concept after all, so some details are sure to have been overlooked.
Photo: Yi-Chen Jung If you do need one, you’ll walk out of the store with a basket of groceries, head over to your chosen or designated Go-Future, toss the basket onto the rear hold we see in the renderings, hop inside the EV , and drive home, or be carried autonomously; it’s not quite clear how we move around just yet.
Speaking of moving, the design also includes all-weather use, or at least, light weather use, with a cabin that does lie mostly open but with the possibility to add a sort of hardtop over the occupant. But the sides of the vehicle are still missing and expose the rider to strong rains, snow, and wind.
All three of the traits above also mean that the Go-Future is not meant for the longest drives out there, but rather, as a vehicle that’s meant to travel a couple of miles at a time, a true last-mile solution. There's no mention of peak range or anything like that.
As a future mobility solution, one that’s designed to decongest our cities by taking shoppers out of busses, subways, or their own cars, Mr. Jung also paid special attention to the body of this EV, and not just by making it a single-occupancy vehicle, but the way it’s made too.
Photo: Yi-Chen Jung According to the ideation board, the Go-Future is to be crafted with a recycled body, at least, the lower half of the shell. If the design ever makes it into a real one that’s displayed at some shows like the Red Dot or iF awards, then it’s bound to get some extra points for reducing plastic waste.
This also marks the Go-Future as a concept that can see life after having carried out its duties and is decommissioned with honor. Just melt down the parts that CAN be melted down and use the goo to mold the shell of a new Go-Future. If you’ve also picked up on the fact that this makes it rather easy to replace broken parts, you’d be spot on.
Mr. Jung also mentions modularity as being part of the EV’s makeup, and from what I could make out, it’s part of the part-replacement ecosystem that Mr. Jung has worked into the design. If something breaks, it’s easy to fix. Color options also fall into the modular side of the story, with multiple available to companies to choose from.
As the saying goes, the plot thickens. The Go-Future is also designed with an app, so Mr. Jung has thought of some of the more important sides of this conceptual story, and it’s an app that is aimed at the fleet operator and the end user too.
Photo: Yi-Chen Jung All this raises one question: just how useful would something like the Go-Future be to the masses? Well, from a decongestion standpoint, this EV is smaller, so it would reduce some footprint. The second aspect that is to be considered is all that eco-friendly and recycled plastics goodness; a big win for any concept these days.
We also need to look at if it makes any sense to flood neighborhoods with these. I mean, if my grocery store is within half a mile or so to my home, I'll probably walk, except if I need some larger items, in which case, I'll call upon a car; larger items seem to be off the menu for the Go-Future too.
Maybe I'll grab a bicycle and a backpack and handle things that way. I mean, cargo e-bikes are really starting to
What I'm trying to say is that it might not make so much sense to create such a vehicle and system considering the extensive network of shops and stores in modern cities. Then again, it doesn’t hurt to dream a little.
